title: String Quartet No. 2 in D major
hook: A chemist’s love letter to his wife, with one of the most famous nocturnes ever written.

painting.title: Moonlit Night
painting.pairingNote: A young woman alone on a bench in a moonlit garden, painted a year before the quartet; a nocturne in paint, for a quartet its composer gave to his wife.

facts: Alexander Borodin was a professor of chemistry first and a composer in his spare time. He was also a keen amateur cellist, and the cello opens two of the four movements here with the main melody.

He wrote the quartet quickly in the summer of 1881, while staying at the country estate of his friend Nikolai Lodyzhensky, south-east of Moscow. It is dedicated to his wife, Ekaterina, a pianist he had met in Heidelberg, where he worked as a young chemist.

Borodin’s biographer Serge Dianin suggested that the quartet was a present for the twentieth anniversary of that meeting, and that it recalls it in music. Borodin left no programme, so this is an interpretation, not a fact.

In 1953 the Broadway musical *Kismet* turned Borodin’s melodies into songs, including the second theme of this quartet’s scherzo (“Baubles, Bangles and Beads”). The show won a Tony Award in 1954, and Borodin, long dead, was among those honoured.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a warm, singing conversation led by the cello (I), a quick, shimmering scherzo with a waltz tune (II), a love song at night (III), a question and an answer that become a race (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro moderato
movements.summary: The cello opens with a long, songful melody high in its range, and the first violin answers. The whole movement is lyrical: instead of dramatic clashes, Borodin gets contrast from changing keys and from lines that weave around each other. It is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]].

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a warm, gently rising melody on the cello, high up, answered by the violin.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a tender tune on the first violin, in A major, with a middle part where violin and cello trade phrases.

notice: Listen to the very first notes. The cello is playing high, almost in the violin’s range, which gives it a singing, tenor-like sound.
When the tender tune returns at ≈ 5:50, it is in the “wrong” key. Listen for the moment, a minute later, when it finds its way home.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The Takács Quartet recorded this in December 1995 in the Protestant church at Honrath, Germany, with Edward Dusinberre and Károly Schranz (violins), Roger Tapping (viola) and András Fejér (cello). On the Spotify album the Borodin is tracks 5–8, after Smetana’s First Quartet, “From My Life”.

movements.heading: Scherzo: Allegro
movements.summary: A fast, light scherzo, placed second rather than third, as Borodin also did in his Second Symphony. A quick, glittering figure on the first violin alternates with a lilting tune that later became a Broadway song. Unusually for a scherzo, it is in sonata form, and it ends in a whisper.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a quick, falling run on the first violin, with a little falling figure in the viola underneath.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a lilting, waltz-like tune built on rising steps, the tune of “Baubles, Bangles and Beads”.

notice: The lilting tune at ≈ 0:25 is built from rising steps; the viola’s little figure in the opening falls. Borodin made one from the other by turning it upside down.
Listen to the end: no big final chord, just a fade.

movements.heading: Notturno: Andante
movements.summary: The quartet’s most famous movement. The cello sings a long, tender song, then the first violin takes it. A more agitated middle section interrupts the calm. When the melody returns, cello and violin play it in [[canon|canon]], one following the other, like two voices in conversation.

mainIdeas.name: The melody
mainIdeas.description: long, warm and slow, first on the cello, over soft, gently pulsing chords.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: quicker, more restless figures and a rising phrase.

In the canon at ≈ 4:20, try to follow both voices: the cello leads, the violin echoes.

movements.heading: Finale: Andante – Vivace
movements.summary: It starts slowly, with a question and an answer: the two violins ask, viola and cello reply. Then the question speeds up and becomes a quick, busy theme passed from player to player. Borodin’s skill with [[counterpoint|counterpoint]] is on show: lines enter one after another and weave together, and the movement races to a broad, bright end in D major.

mainIdeas.name: The Vivace theme
mainIdeas.description: the question at speed, entering in turn on viola, second violin and first violin.

threads.title: The cello
threads.body: Borodin played it himself, and it opens both the first movement and the Notturno with the main melody.

threads.title: Lyrical, not dramatic
threads.body: Contrast comes from changing keys and woven lines more than from conflict.

threads.title: Pairs
threads.body: Question and answer in the finale, the canon in the Notturno, the violin answering the cello in the first movement: the quartet is full of conversations for two.

threads.title: A love letter?
threads.body: The dedication to Ekaterina is a fact; the story of the first meeting is Dianin’s reading. Listen and decide.
